content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe the pH scale and what it measures
Relate pH to hydrogen ion concentration
Identify substances as acidic, neutral, or alkaline from pH
is a way of measuring how acidic or alkaline a solution is. It runs from 0 to 14, with 7 being neutral. pH is one of the most important measurements in chemistry and biology.
is a measure of the hydrogen ion (H⁺) concentration in a solution.
Each pH unit represents a 10-fold change in H⁺ concentration
pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4
pH 3 is 100× more acidic than pH 5
[DIAGRAM: pH colour chart showing red (pH 1-3), orange (4), yellow (5-6), green (7), blue (8-9), purple (10-14)]

H⁺ ions react with OH⁻: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O
A solution has pH 4. Is it acidic, neutral, or alkaline? How does its H⁺ concentration compare to a solution of pH 6?
pH 4 is less than 7, so it is
pH 4 is 2 units lower than pH 6
A student adds sodium hydroxide solution to hydrochloric acid and measures the pH throughout. The initial pH is 1. What happens to the pH as the alkali is added?
As NaOH is added, OH⁻ reacts with H⁺
If more NaOH is added, pH continues to rise above 7
pH could reach 13-14 with excess NaOH
Solution A has pH 3 and solution B has pH 5. How many times more acidic is solution A?
Explain why universal indicator is used instead of litmus when you need to know the pH of a solution.
Litmus only shows acidic (red) or alkaline (blue)
It cannot distinguish between different acidities
Universal indicator shows a range of colours
Each colour corresponds to a different pH value
This allows you to determine the approximate pH
For example, you can tell pH 2 from pH 5 (both acidic but different colours)
Thinking lower pH means less acidic
Lower pH means MORE acidic (more H⁺)
Thinking pH 14 is twice as alkaline as pH 7
The scale is logarithmic, not linear
Assuming all neutral solutions have pH exactly 7
Some neutral salt solutions may have slightly different pH
